{"id": "20:81/q15", "question": "How are the two verbs for wrath read, and what do their forms mean?", "turns_on": "The transmitted vowels and constructions, and whether the verb depicts a due claim, descent, or a caused descent.", "positions": [{"id": "20:81/q15/p1", "position": "Both verbs use kasra, conveying wrath becoming due, arriving, or overtaking.", "reasons": "The majority reading is reported by al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Mujāhid, al-Fārisī and others. Al-Naḥḥās and Ibn Khālawayh prefer it by the parallel of a lasting punishment becoming due (cited as 22:4); al-Farrāʾ favors its fit with obligation; al-Qurṭubī cites 11:39. Al-Fārisī also says kasra evokes permissibility and arrival, citing 16:1, 29:54, 10:24, 11:39 and 20:86. Al-Wāḥidī says 'becomes due' describes lifted protection and ensuing punishment rather than a literal lexical definition; several compare a payable debt (2:196)."}, {"id": "20:81/q15/p2", "position": "Both verbs use ḍamma, conveying wrath descending, alighting, or settling.", "reasons": "Al-Kisāʾī is repeatedly singled out, with al-Aʿmash, Yaḥyā b. Waththāb, Qatāda, Abū Ḥaywa and Ṭalḥa also transmitted. Al-Fārisī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Wāḥidī explain descent through punishment that follows anger (13:31); al-Biqāʿī notes forceful settling. Qiraat-ER distinguishes a root for settling from one for descending, contrary to sources that gloss ḍamma as descent; al-Miṣbāḥ allows both vocalizations for punishment."}, {"id": "20:81/q15/p3", "position": "Kasra and ḍamma are both sound and closely related in meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī accepts both famous readings because disobedience makes wrath both descend and become due; al-Qurṭubī calls them dialect forms, and al-Wāḥidī says protection lifts so punishment arrives."}, {"id": "20:81/q15/p4", "position": "A mixed kasra and ḍamma form is transmitted.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and Abū Ḥayyān attribute a mixed form to Ibn ʿUtayba; al-Rāzī reports al-Aʿmash from ʿAbd Allāh's companions with first kasra and second nominative; al-Ālūsī notes Ibn ʿUtba agrees in the latter vowel."}, {"id": "20:81/q15/p5", "position": "A prohibitive lā with emphatic nūn warns them not to expose themselves to wrath.", "reasons": "Ibn Ghazwān reports this from Ṭalḥa; al-Samīn compares 'I must not see you here', and al-Ālūsī specifies fatḥa on lām and kasra on ḥāʾ."}, {"id": "20:81/q15/p6", "position": "A causative reading makes transgression bring wrath down, or implies God as agent with punishment omitted.", "reasons": "Al-Lawāmiʿ reports Qatāda, ʿAbd Allāh b. Muslim b. Yasār, Ibn Waththāb and al-Aʿmash. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī give the alternative omitted object."}]}
{"id": "20:81/q16", "question": "What is the subject of the verb when wrath descends?", "turns_on": "Whether wrath functions as subject or object in the causative analysis.", "positions": [{"id": "20:81/q16/p1", "position": "My wrath is the subject in either ordinary reading.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn calls this the prevailing analysis and objects to al-Lawāmiʿ's exclusion; on a causative account, an omitted object is possible with wrath as subject."}, {"id": "20:81/q16/p2", "position": "My wrath is the object, with transgression an omitted subject.", "reasons": "Al-Lawāmiʿ considers transgression obvious; al-Samīn calls that restriction awkward because causative iḥlāl takes one object and wrath can instead be subject with another object omitted."}]}
{"id": "20:81/q17", "question": "Why is one doubled verb assimilated and the other written distinctly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:81/q17/p1", "position": "Assimilation depends on adjacent lām consonants both moving; the other form keeps a still second lām after vowel transfer.", "reasons": "Ibn Khālawayh gives the consonant movement; Ibn Mālik says undoubled clarity such as yaḥlil is Hijazi usage, while assimilation is Tamimi."}]}
{"id": "20:81/q18", "question": "What does God's wrath mean here?", "turns_on": "How language of human anger and physical descent applies to God's wrath.", "positions": [{"id": "20:81/q18/p1", "position": "It is divine punishment, vengeance, or torment, rather than bodily anger.", "reasons": "Muqātil and al-Qurṭubī equate anger with punishment; al-Bursawī excludes heart agitation. Al-Ālūsī cites a hadith describing human anger as heated blood, swollen veins and red eyes, then says God’s wrath suits His majesty and may mean punishment, vengeance, or willing either. Asad describes unavoidable retribution for deliberate rejection and injustice."}, {"id": "20:81/q18/p2", "position": "It is an active attribute realized by willing harm through causes after disobedience.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī describes anger's realization and compares wrath becoming payable to a debt."}, {"id": "20:81/q18/p3", "position": "In inward reading, it is deprivation and abandonment after spiritual failure.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī connects abandonment to one sin following another, missing regret, or accepting a lower state; al-Qāshānī says deprivation follows egoic self-display."}, {"id": "20:81/q18/p4", "position": "Calling divine wrath a 'descent' may name an effect by the will that causes it.", "reasons": "Al-Intiṣāf, reported by al-Ālūsī, says a will of punishment cannot itself descend; one may interpret suitably, as with reports of divine descent, or speak of its effect. Al-Ālūsī says the verb can be literal or figurative by reading."}]}
{"id": "20:81/q19", "question": "What does the warning teach about grave sin and spiritual loss?", "turns_on": "The doctrinal and inward implications drawn from falling under wrath.", "positions": [{"id": "20:81/q19/p1", "position": "A grave sinner deserves punishment, contrary to the Murjiʾa.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī explicitly argues from the fall under divine anger against the Murjiʾa."}, {"id": "20:81/q19/p2", "position": "Spiritual arrogance can nullify devotional dealings and cast the servant from nearness.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī ties the warning to ecstatic claims of lordship, urges guidance through 1:6; al-Qāshānī says the spirit falls into the self's hell and is veiled from beauty."}]}
{"id": "20:81/q20", "question": "What does 'he has fallen' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the fall names ruin generally, wretchedness, worldly loss, Hell's abyss, or spiritual exile.", "positions": [{"id": "20:81/q20/p1", "position": "He perished or was destroyed, an image from a fatal fall.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba cites hawat ummuhu; al-Wāḥidī cites al-Nābigha and Kaʿb b. Saʿd for death, while al-Kashshāf cites a poem on a crushing mountain fall. Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites an eagle and falling bucket; Ibn al-Jawzī gives hawā yahwī and a pit. Abū Ḥayyān explains the euphemism as calamity after safety."}, {"id": "20:81/q20/p2", "position": "He falls into Hell, its Fire, or its abyss al-Hāwiya.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj says he reaches Hell's depths; al-Wāḥidī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya report the abyss explanation; al-Ṭabrisī derives the sense from a fall from height. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Wāḥidī's Wajīz and Elmalılı describe the abyss."}, {"id": "20:81/q20/p3", "position": "He has become wretched.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is reported by al-Wāḥidī and Ibn Kathīr; al-Rāzī and al-Suyūṭī also give this gloss."}, {"id": "20:81/q20/p4", "position": "He has perished in this world.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī records this as an alternative to falling into the Fire."}, {"id": "20:81/q20/p5", "position": "He falls from divine nearness into the ego's hell, veiled from beauty.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī's inward explanation joins deprivation to the fall."}]}
{"id": "20:81/q21", "question": "What Hell images are reported for this fall?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:81/q21/p1", "position": "A palace in Hell receives a falling unbeliever for forty years.", "reasons": "Shafī al-Aṣbaḥī's report pairs a palace named Hawā with a mountain named Suʿūd climbed for forty years and links 74:17. Al-Ālūsī relays an unnamed palace report; Ibn Kathīr transmits Shafī b. Mātiʿ through Ibn Abī Ḥātim, with a high castle and baked clay at the bottom."}]}
{"id": "20:81/q22", "question": "How is the warning situated among the surrounding blessings and verses?", "turns_on": "Which surrounding events and verse links illustrate the warning.", "positions": [{"id": "20:81/q22/p1", "position": "The passage moves from rescue, to revelation, to worldly food, to a ban and accepted repentance.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī put removal of harm first, religious benefit above worldly benefit, and provision last; al-Kuranyolu draws the universal lesson to enjoy without excess, seek forgiveness and never despair of mercy."}, {"id": "20:81/q22/p2", "position": "Israel's desire for other foods and later idolatry show the warned ingratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Study Quran invoke 2:61 for the food complaint; Study Quran adds 7:138–141 and 20:87–88 for the later idol episodes."}]}
{"id": "20:81/q23", "question": "Why can an omitted pronoun sharpen expression near the word for wrath?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:81/q23/p1", "position": "Ellipsis can make a line more graceful than overtly restoring its subject.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī's general point uses Ibn al-Zubayr's omitted huwa before dāsiʿ nafsihi and Bakr b. al-Naṭṭāḥ's ghaḍbā omitting hiya before or after the adjective; pronouncing it spoils the effect."}]}
{"id": "20:81/q24", "question": "What authority governs reports and interpretation of this warning?", "turns_on": "The relationship of transmitted boundaries and reflective insight.", "positions": [{"id": "20:81/q24/p1", "position": "Its occasion and story require verified transmission, while interpretation must respect transmitted limits.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī says tafsīr uncovers circumstances like a physician examining a urine sample; taʾwīl means returning a sense to its source. Recitation stays within written Qur'an and interpretation within transmitted knowledge, though God can open insight through contemplation."}, {"id": "20:81/q24/p2", "posi

{"id": "20:81/q25", "question": "How can a verse have an outer and inner aspect, a limit, and an opening?", "turns_on": "How the transmitted outer/inner and boundary/opening terms are interpreted.", "positions": [{"id": "20:81/q25/p1", "position": "Each verse or letter has outer and inner aspects and a boundary with a point of ascent.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī reports Ibn Masʿūd's seven-aḥruf wording, without grading; al-Suyūṭī gives a stopped Ibn Masʿūd report on each letter's boundary and opening. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk transmits Ibn ʿAbbās on inexhaustible branches and the need to study scholars rather than fools."}, {"id": "20:81/q25/p2", "position": "Outer is the wording or recitation; inner is interpretation or understanding.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī and al-Suyūṭī report this formulation; another says reflection compares inner sense to wording; a further version says recitation is as revealed and inner understanding follows contemplation (73:4; 38:29). Ibn al-Naqīb says inner secrets are disclosed to spiritual adepts."}, {"id": "20:81/q25/p3", "position": "Outer historical stories warn later readers inwardly not to repeat past disobedience.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī gives this view; Abū ʿUbayd judges it the soundest; Ibn Masʿūd says each verse has been enacted before and will be enacted again."}, {"id": "20:81/q25/p4", "position": "A verse's limit may be intended meaning, lawful and unlawful rulings, or its deserved reward or punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī gives the alternatives; al-Baghawī calls each letter bounded in recitation and interpretation."}, {"id": "20:81/q25/p5", "position": "Its opening may be a route to hidden meaning, understanding, or the unveiling of reward and punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī defines maṭlaʿ as ascent to knowledge; al-Suyūṭī gives routes to difficult senses and rulings, afterlife disclosure, and insight into promise and threat."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q01", "question": "Who is speaking?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q01/p1", "position": "Aaron speaks to Moses after Moses returns to the calf worship.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies the brothers; Yaḥyā places the rebuke on Moses' return."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q02", "question": "How is يَبْنَؤُمَّ read and analyzed?", "turns_on": "The mīm vowel, compounding and omission of a possessive ending.", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q02/p1", "position": "The mīm has fatḥa, explained as a fused vocative or shortened yā ibn ummā.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid and Fārisī list Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Ḥafṣ; Jishumī adds Abū Jaʿfar. Naḥḥās compares a fused noun; Fārisī, Jishumī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya compare khamsata ʿashar or lost alif; Bursevī traces ummī through ummā."}, {"id": "20:94/q02/p2", "position": "The mīm has kasra, a genitive construction with omitted possessive yāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid and Fārisī assign this to Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, Kisāʾī and Ibn ʿĀmir; Naṣafī says Syrian and Kufan readers except Ḥafṣ. Fārisī also permits a compound; Jishumī cites ibn ʿamm and yā ghulām; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the yāʾ loss irregular. QIRAAT-ER notes overt genitive inflection."}, {"id": "20:94/q02/p3", "position": "A form with explicit possessive yāʾ is also attested.", "reasons": "Abū Isḥāq permits non-Quranic yā ibna ummī; QIRAAT-ER records a possessive variant."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q03", "question": "Why does Aaron say 'son of my mother'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q03/p1", "position": "He appeals to kinship and maternal tenderness to calm Moses.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Ibn Kathīr, Biqāʿī, Bursevī, Ālūsī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī give this motive; Biqāʿī notes maternal pain. Burhān and Itqān call it affectionate address; Burhān links the renewed vocative to emotional distance."}, {"id": "20:94/q03/p2", "position": "In an inward reading it recalls mercy and Moses' Sinai encounter.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports Sufi masters linking maternal nurture to Aaron's merciful prophethood (19:53); Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya describes Moses' longing, collapse and angels dragging his head, with Ḥāfiẓ's Sīmurgh image of a lofty station."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q04", "question": "What was the brothers' parentage?", "turns_on": "Literal genealogy versus rhetorical maternal appeal.", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q04/p1", "position": "They shared both parents.", "reasons": "Often called the majority view; the maternal address is then tender rather than a literal distinction."}, {"id": "20:94/q04/p2", "position": "They shared only a mother.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī, Wāḥidī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Rāzī and Bayḍāwī report it; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it weak and Ālūsī rejects it as the explanation."}, {"id": "20:94/q04/p3", "position": "They shared a father but not a mother.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports this contradictory alternative."}, {"id": "20:94/q04/p4", "position": "Motherhood is literal, fatherhood a legal attribution.", "reasons": "Thaʿlabī transmits this further account."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q05", "question": "What is notable about the written vocative and its parallel?", "turns_on": "Orthography and degree of narrative detail.", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q05/p1", "position": "The connected spelling varies in retained alifs.", "reasons": "Itqān describes joined ibn umm, hamza written as wāw and omitted ibn hamza; Nashr says al-Dānī saw both alifs lost while the author saw codices retaining one."}, {"id": "20:94/q05/p2", "position": "The fuller Ṭāhā wording uses a vocative particle for narrative detail or emphasis.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī contrasts the concise al-Aʿrāf report; his notes phrase the direction inconsistently but cite clarity, detail and emphasis."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q06", "question": "What do the beard and head designate, and how is 'beard' read?", "turns_on": "Anatomical reference and dialectal vocalization.", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q06/p1", "position": "Beard means chin hair; head means its hair or forelock.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī define beard; Thaʿlabī calls these honored parts; Wāḥidī, Baghawī and Biqāʿī identify head hair. Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn note variant plural vowels."}, {"id": "20:94/q06/p2", "position": "Head can stand for Aaron's ear.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports a view that Moses held ear and beard."}, {"id": "20:94/q06/p3", "position": "The beard's lām has the usual kasra.", "reasons": "Samīn calls it the eloquent majority form."}, {"id": "20:94/q06/p4", "position": "The beard's lām has fatḥa in a Hijazi reading.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn and Ālūsī attribute it to ʿĪsā ibn Sulaymān."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q07", "question": "What is the bāʾ in 'by my beard' doing?", "turns_on": "Whether the particle is grammatically extra.", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q07/p1", "position": "It is extra for emphasis.", "reasons": "Jishumī compares bi-junūdihi and 17:1; Samīn rejects this as overreach, comparing 2:195."}, {"id": "20:94/q07/p2", "position": "It contributes to the construction, or follows an omitted object 'me'.", "reasons": "Samīn supplies both analyses and rejects the extra-bāʾ view."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q08", "question": "Did Moses seize Aaron, and for what purpose?", "turns_on": "What occurred and what Moses intended.", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q08/p1", "position": "He grasped head hair and beard in anger over idolatry or Aaron's apparent lapse.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Kalbī and reports specify right hand on hair and left on beard; Ibn Kathīr says he cast tablets and dragged Aaron. Māwardī prefers reproach for insufficient condemnation; Ibn al-Anbārī says Moses thought Aaron disobeyed; Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ālūsī and Islāḥī emphasize religious zeal. Ṭabāṭabāʾī suggests an intended strike."}, {"id": "20:94/q08/p2", "position": "He drew Aaron near without contempt, as one handles oneself in agitation.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Qurṭubī compare holding one's own beard; Rāzī compares twisting fingers and stresses brotherly identification."}, {"id": "20:94/q08/p3", "position": "He wished to whisper about the tablets or investigate privately.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports the whispering account; Rāzī says Israel's suspicion, even an accusation that Moses killed Aaron, framed the investigation."}, {"id": "20:94/q08/p4", "position": "He suspected Aaron supported the calf worshipers.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports and rejects this as impermissible of prophets."}, {"id": "20:94/q08/p5", "position": "The prohibition alone does not prove a completed seizure.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites prohibitions at 33:48 and 39:65; he distinguishes the separate report of head-pulling."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q09", "question": "Why did Aaron ask Moses to stop?", "turns_on": "How the gesture appeared to Aaron and Israel.", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q09/p1", "position": "Observers might mistake it for contempt, punishment or rejection.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās, Qurṭubī's Ibn ʿAbbās and Rāzī cite possible misreading by a suspicious people."}, {"id": "20:94/q09/p2", "position": "He sought to end an angry or threatening gesture.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Bayḍāwī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī describe angry seizure; Ṭabāṭabāʾī suggests a blow."}, {"id": "20:94/q09/p3", "position": "The local custom treated beard-taking like taking a hand.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī says it was not then humiliating and that custom determines assessment."}]}

{"id": "20:94/q11", "question": "What division did Aaron fear?", "turns_on": "Whether departure, fighting or existing belief was the decisive cause.", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q11/p1", "position": "Leaving with believers for Moses would separate them from the calf's remaining followers.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd and Ibn ʿAbbās report this; Ṭabarī prefers it because Aaron urged the people and they refused (20:90–91). Naḥḥās, Wāḥidī, Qurṭubī and Ibn Kathīr give similar accounts; Islāḥī adds Sāmirī's sway and Aaron's fear."}, {"id": "20:94/q11/p2", "position": "Forceful confrontation would split factions and cause killing.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn Jurayj and many later authors give this; Wāḥidī describes believers, calf followers and Sāmirī's party; Biqāʿī cites few weak allies and retaliation; Ālūsī fears lasting separation. Qatāda recalls earlier righteous people disliking division."}, {"id": "20:94/q11/p3", "position": "Different beliefs had already divided the people.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports this account."}, {"id": "20:94/q11/p4", "position": "Moses would himself be blamed for splitting them through fighting or separate followings.", "reasons": "Māwardī mentions fighting; Nasafī's wording attributes separation to Moses' action."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q12", "question": "What was Moses' earlier instruction?", "turns_on": "Departure versus stewardship under changed circumstances.", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q12/p1", "position": "Remain deputy, reform, preserve unity and await Moses' return.", "reasons": "Muqātil and later authors invoke 7:142; Biqāʿī says it did not require the sword and compares gentle resistance; Ālūsī cites Aaron's near killing (7:150). Rāzī makes following conditional on avoiding disorder; Asad reports Zamakhsharī on unity. Durr says Aaron stayed among the believers, listening and obeying, because he feared Moses would accuse him of dividing Israel and failing to observe his instruction."}, {"id": "20:94/q12/p2", "position": "Follow Moses with believers.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī prefers this account of Moses' reproach; Aaron feared abandoning the rest."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q13", "question": "What does 'you did not heed my word' mean?", "turns_on": "Preserving versus awaiting, and whose words are meant.", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q13/p1", "position": "You did not observe, preserve or enact my instruction.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Ṭabarī derive it from watchful attention; Muqātil and others tie it to care for the people. Jishumī notes raqīb and mirqab; Asad glosses qawlī as what Moses said; Nasafī sees scope for juristic reasoning."}, {"id": "20:94/q13/p2", "position": "You did not wait for my instruction, return or decision.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda, Ibn Jurayj and al-ʿUyūn give waiting; Taʾwīlāt says Aaron waited obediently; al-ʿUyūn also offers consideration of Moses' situation."}, {"id": "20:94/q13/p3", "position": "Moses did not await Aaron's own explanation.", "reasons": "Ālūsī transmits Ibn Jurayj's shifted implied speaker."}]}
{"id": "20:94/q14", "question": "How is the final clause construed and read?", "turns_on": "Coordination versus circumstance; a separate variant changes the verb form.", "positions": [{"id": "20:94/q14/p1", "position": "It coordinates with farraqta as a second feared accusation.", "reasons": "Samīn calls it accusative; Ālūsī reports the same."}, {"id": "20:94/q14/p2", "position": "It is circumstantial: division happened without awaiting Moses' instruction.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this alternative."}, {"id": "20:94/q14/p3", "position": "It is circumstantial with Aaron's own speech implied.", "reasons": "Ālūsī cites Ibn Jurayj: Moses spoke without awaiting Aaron's clarification."}, {"id": "20:94/q14/p4", "position": "Abū Jaʿfar reads turqib from arqaba.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, Samīn and Ālūsī specify ḍamma on the prefix and kasra on qāf."}]}

{"id": "20:130/q01", "question": "What speech must the Prophet endure, and why?", "turns_on": "Whether the command is read primarily against the opponents' speech and its delayed punishment or as inward formation under divine decree.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q01/p1", "position": "He must endure hostile denials, insults, and demands for punishment until God's appointed judgment, while continuing his mission.", "reasons": "Muqatil specifies denial of threatened punishment; Yahya, Tabari, Mawardi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Razi, Bursevi and Ibn Ashur list accusations including sorcery, madness, poetry, lying and soothsaying. {"id": "20:130/q02", "question": "What does patience mean here as a virtue?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q02/p1", "position": "It is self-restraint appropriate to reason and divine law, expressed differently in battle, calamity, and silence; enduring abuse can be good or obligatory.", "reasons": "Bursevi quotes Raghib's definition and his examples of courage, broadness of chest and keeping silent, with 2:177, 22:35 and 33:35; Jishumi says endurance of abuse is praiseworthy and sometimes obligatory."}]}
{"id": "20:130/q03", "question": "Was the command to endure their speech abrogated by fighting?", "turns_on": "Whether patient endurance of speech is incompatible with the later command to fight.", "positions": [{"id": "20:130/q03/p1", "position": "Yes; the later fighting command ended the earlier permission or duty simply to endure abuse.", "reasons": "Wahidi says God subsequently decreed their killing; Ibn Jawzi and the reported Kalbi-Muqatil, Baghawi and Bursevi accounts cite the fighting or sword verse."}, {"id": "20:130/q03/p2", "position": "No; combat and patience under verbal abuse can coexist, so the command remains applicable.", "reasons": "Jishumi argues that the passages do not conflict; Qurtubi reports that fighting did not eradicate all unbelievers; al-Kabir says fighting need not end endurance of speech; Alusi reads patience as composure, not cessation of fighting."}]}
